title: Population and Culture
bigQuestion: Why do people live where they live, speak what they speak, and move when they move?

story.title: Two Pyramids, Side by Side
story.kicker: A demographer lays two charts on a desk. One looks like a pine tree. The other looks like a kite with a wide top. Each is a country's future drawn in bars.
paragraphs: A population pyramid is a simple chart. Down the middle runs a list of ages, from babies at the bottom to people over one hundred at the top. To the left, a bar shows how many males are in each age group. To the right, a bar shows the females. Stack the bars and you get a shape. The shape tells a story that a single number, like total population, cannot.

The first chart is Nigeria. Its bottom bars are enormous and each step up is shorter than the one below. Almost half of Nigerians are under eighteen, and the median age, the age that splits the country into two equal halves, is about eighteen. Women in Nigeria have, on average, roughly five children each. A chart like this is a country full of schools, first jobs, and young families. It is also a country that must build a classroom and a clinic faster than almost anywhere on Earth.

The second chart is Japan. Its bottom bars are narrow. The widest bars sit near ages fifty and seventy, and the top does not taper to a point but stays thick, because many Japanese live past ninety. The median age is close to forty-nine. Women there have, on average, about one and a third children. This is a country where more people die each year than are born, where villages empty out, and where the question is who will care for the old and who will pay for it.

Neither shape is a mistake. Each is the result of choices made by millions of families over decades, shaped by medicine, jobs, schools, and what it costs to raise a child. And each shape carries momentum. Nigeria will keep growing for years even if birth rates fall tomorrow, because so many of its people have not yet had children. Japan will keep shrinking even if births rise, because so few of its people are of child-bearing age.

Human geography is the study of people in place: where they are, how many, who they are, what they believe, what they speak, and why they move. Those two pyramids are a starting point. By the end of this chapter you should be able to look at a chart like that and see the schools, the pensions, the migrants, and the arguments hidden in the bars.
story.think: If you were the education minister of Nigeria, what would you build first? If you were the health minister of Japan? What would each of you worry about in twenty years?

lessons.title: Where Eight Billion People Live
lessons.mainIdea: People are spread very unevenly across the Earth, and the pattern follows water, soil, climate and history.
reading: In November of 2022 the United Nations announced that the world's population had passed eight billion. That number is hard to picture, so start with a map. Shade every square where people live and most of the planet stays blank. Antarctica has no permanent residents. The Sahara, central Australia, Siberia, and the high plateau of Tibet hold almost no one. Meanwhile a few patches glow: the plains of eastern China, the Ganges valley of India, the island of Java, western Europe, and the eastern United States.

Geographers use *population density* to describe this. Density is simply people divided by land area. Bangladesh packs more than a thousand people into each square kilometer. Canada, which is far larger, averages about four. Illinois falls in between, with roughly ninety. But density hides as much as it shows. Most of Canada's people live within a couple hundred miles of the U.S. border, and most of Illinois lives in the Chicago area, so a single average for the whole state is misleading.

Why the pattern? People cluster where they can grow food and reach one another. River valleys with rich soil fed the earliest cities, and they still hold huge numbers. Coasts allow trade. Mild climates with enough rain make farming reliable. Deserts, tundra, and steep mountains push people away. History then locks the pattern in: a city that grew because of a river keeps growing long after trains and trucks replace the boats, because the people, buildings and jobs are already there.

The word *ecumene* means the part of the Earth that people permanently inhabit. Over thousands of years the ecumene has spread as people learned to irrigate deserts, heat homes in the far north, and drain swamps. Chicago itself was built on marshy ground beside a sluggish river. Engineers raised whole streets and buildings by several feet in the 1850s and 1860s to make the city drain. Where people live is partly nature's choice and partly ours.

words.d: the number of people living in a given area, usually per square mile or square kilometer
the portion of the Earth's surface that people permanently live on
the statistical study of human populations: their size, growth, age and movement

look.title: How Crowded Is It?
look.cite: World Bank and U.S. Census, roughly 2020, rounded
look.prompt: Australia and Canada are both huge and mostly empty. What do their empty parts have in common, and how is it different in each?

check.q: What is population density?
choices: The number of people per unit of land area
The total number of people in a country
The number of cities in a region
The rate at which a population grows
check.why: Density divides people by land area, so it measures how crowded a place is rather than how many people it has in total.

check.q: Why can a country's average density be misleading?
choices: Because the census never counts rural areas
Because people are often clustered in a few parts of it
Because land area changes every year
Because density only counts adults
check.why: Canada and Illinois both average out large empty areas with crowded ones, so the average describes almost nowhere in particular.

check.q: Which region would you expect to have very LOW population density?
choices: The Ganges valley in India
The eastern United States
The high plateau of Tibet
The island of Java
check.why: Tibet is cold, dry and very high, so it grows little food and supports few people. The other three are warm, wet, fertile lowlands.

lessons.title: The Demographic Transition
lessons.mainIdea: As countries industrialize, death rates fall first and birth rates fall later, and the gap between them produces a burst of population growth.
reading: For most of human history, populations barely grew. Families had many children, but many of those children died young, and famine and disease killed adults too. High births and high deaths canceled out. Then, starting in Britain around 1800 and spreading across the world, something changed. Clean water, sewers, vaccines, and better food made death rates fall. But birth rates did not fall at the same time. For a generation or two, families kept having six or seven children, and most of them now lived.

Geographers call this pattern the *demographic transition*, and they describe it in stages. In stage one, births and deaths are both high and the population is stable. In stage two, deaths drop while births stay high, and the population explodes. In stage three, births begin to fall as children survive, cities grow, and women get schooling and jobs. In stage four, births and deaths are both low and growth slows to almost nothing. Some geographers add a stage five, where births fall below deaths and the population shrinks, as in Japan and Italy today.

The model explains why the world grew so fast in the twentieth century. In 1900 there were about 1.6 billion people. By 2000 there were about 6.1 billion. That was not because people suddenly had more children. It was because far fewer of them died. Countries went through stage two one after another: Europe first, then Latin America and Asia, and much of sub-Saharan Africa now. Nigeria's pyramid is a stage-two or early stage-three shape. Japan's is stage five.

The *total fertility rate*, or TFR, is the key number. It is the average number of children a woman will have over her lifetime. A TFR of about 2.1 keeps a population steady, because each pair of parents is replaced by two children with a little extra for those who die young. The world's TFR fell from about five in 1960 to about 2.3 today. The United States sits near 1.6, Illinois close to that, so American growth now comes mainly from immigration rather than births.

words.d: the shift from high birth and death rates to low ones as a society industrializes, with rapid growth in between
the average number of children a woman would have over her lifetime at current birth rates
a fertility rate of about 2.1 children per woman, which keeps a population the same size over time

look.title: Malthus Sounds the Alarm
look.text: Population, when unchecked, increases in a geometrical ratio. Subsistence increases only in an arithmetical ratio.
look.cite: Thomas Malthus, An Essay on the Principle of Population, 1798
look.prompt: Malthus feared population would always outrun food. World population has grown eightfold since he wrote, yet famine has become rarer. What did he miss?

check.q: In the demographic transition, which change happens FIRST?
choices: Birth rates fall
Women stop having children
The population shrinks
Death rates fall
check.why: Clean water, vaccines and better food cut deaths before families change how many children they have, and that gap produces rapid growth.

check.q: Why did world population grow so fast in the twentieth century?
choices: Many more children and adults survived than before
Families began having far more children than before
Countries stopped counting deaths
The world's land area increased
check.why: The reading explains growth came from falling death rates, not rising births. Families kept their old size while far more members lived.

check.q: A country has a total fertility rate of 1.3. Without immigration, what will happen to its population over time?
choices: It will grow quickly
It will shrink
It will stay exactly the same
It will double every generation
check.why: Replacement is about 2.1. A rate of 1.3 means each generation is smaller than the one before, as in Japan.

lessons.title: Reading a Population Pyramid
lessons.mainIdea: A population pyramid shows a country's age and sex structure, and its shape reveals past events and future needs.
reading: A *population pyramid* is really a bar chart turned on its side and folded in the middle. Each horizontal bar is an age group, usually five years wide. Males extend to the left, females to the right. The youngest are at the bottom. Three shapes appear over and over. A wide base and a narrow top means many children and rapid growth. Straight sides mean slow growth, with each age group about the same size. A narrow base and a thick middle or top means an aging, shrinking population.

The bars also record history. Look at Germany's pyramid and you see dents where the two world wars killed young men and cut births. Look at China's and you see a sudden narrowing below age forty-five. That is the mark of the one-child policy, which ran from 1980 to 2015. The United States pyramid has a bulge for people born between 1946 and 1964, the *baby boom* that followed World War II. That bulge is now moving into the top of the chart as those Americans retire.

Planners read pyramids to see what is coming. A wide base means a country needs schools now and jobs in fifteen years. A bulge in the twenties and thirties means a large workforce, which economists call a demographic dividend if the country can employ them. A thick top means rising costs for pensions and health care, with fewer workers to pay for them. The *dependency ratio* compares the number of children and retirees to the number of working-age adults. Both Nigeria and Japan have high ratios, but for opposite reasons.

Notice one more detail. In most countries the bars for women get longer than the bars for men at the oldest ages, because women on average live several years longer. In a few countries, including India and China, the bars for young boys are longer than for young girls, a sign that families have favored sons. A pyramid cannot tell you why, but it can tell you where to look.

words.d: a chart showing how many males and females a population has in each age group
the surge in American births between 1946 and 1964, after World War II
the number of children and older people compared with the number of working-age adults who support them

look.title: Median Age Around the World
look.cite: United Nations population estimates, about 2022, rounded
look.prompt: Half of Niger's people are fifteen or younger. What does that country need most in the next ten years, and what would be the hardest part of paying for it?

check.q: A population pyramid with a very wide base and a narrow top shows a country that is
choices: Stable with equal age groups
Shrinking with many old people
Growing rapidly with many children
Losing young adults to war
check.why: Wide bottom bars mean many young children, which is the signature of rapid growth.

check.q: What caused the bulge in the United States pyramid for people born between 1946 and 1964?
choices: A wave of immigration from Europe
A drop in the death rate among the elderly
The one-child policy
The baby boom after World War II
check.why: The reading names this group the baby boom, a surge in births that followed the war.

check.q: Why does Japan have a high dependency ratio?
choices: It has many retirees compared with working-age adults
Most of its workers have emigrated
It has an unusually large number of children
Its census does not count women
check.why: Japan's pyramid is thick at the top, so retirees outnumber the workers who support them. Nigeria's ratio is high because of children instead.

lessons.title: Push, Pull and the Costs Between
lessons.mainIdea: People migrate when something pushes them from home, something pulls them elsewhere, and the obstacles in between are not too high.
reading: In 1885 an English geographer named Ernst Ravenstein studied the British census and wrote down what he called laws of migration. Most migrants, he found, move only a short distance. Those who go far tend to head for big cities. Every flow of migrants produces a smaller flow back the other way. People from the countryside move more than city people, and young adults move most of all. His laws have held up surprisingly well for almost a century and a half.

In 1966 the American demographer Everett Lee gave the idea a simpler shape. Every place has *push factors* that drive people out: no jobs, war, drought, persecution, a flood. Every place has *pull factors* that draw people in: work, safety, family already there, good land, freedom. Between origin and destination lie intervening obstacles: distance, cost, a border, a sea, a language. A person migrates when the pushes and pulls together outweigh the obstacles. Change any of the three and the flow changes.

Geographers also sort migration by type. Internal migration is within one country, like a family moving from rural Illinois to Chicago. International migration crosses a border. Voluntary migration is chosen, even if the choice is hard. Forced migration is not: the Atlantic slave trade, the removal of Native nations along the Trail of Tears in the 1830s, and today's refugees fleeing war are all forced. The United Nations counts a *refugee* as someone who has crossed a border to escape persecution or violence and cannot safely return.

One more pattern matters. Migrants rarely spread out at random. They follow relatives and neighbors to places where someone they know already lives, which is called chain migration. That is why Chicago has a Polish neighborhood, a Mexican neighborhood on the Southwest Side, and Devon Avenue on the North Side lined with Indian and Pakistani shops. Each chain started with a few people who wrote home and said: come.

words.d: a condition that drives people to leave a place, such as war, unemployment or drought
a condition that attracts people to a place, such as jobs, safety or family
a person forced to cross a border to escape persecution, war or violence
migration in which people follow relatives or neighbors who moved earlier to the same place

look.title: Ravenstein's Laws
look.text: Ravenstein reported that most migrants travel only a short distance, that those going long distances prefer great centers of industry and commerce, that each main current of migration produces a compensating counter-current, and that natives of towns are less migratory than those of rural areas.
look.cite: Ernst Ravenstein, The Laws of Migration, 1885 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Ravenstein used census tables from the 1880s. Which of his laws do you think still holds today, and which might the airplane and the internet have changed?

check.q: A farm family leaves after three years of drought. Drought is an example of a
choices: Pull factor
Push factor
Intervening obstacle
Counter-current
check.why: Drought drives the family out of where they are, which is what a push factor does.

check.q: Which of these is an intervening obstacle in Lee's model?
choices: A job offer in the destination
A war in the origin
The cost of an ocean crossing
Relatives already living in the destination
check.why: Obstacles lie between origin and destination and make the move harder. Cost, distance and borders are the classic ones.

check.q: Why do Chicago's immigrant neighborhoods tend to gather people from the same country?
choices: The city assigns immigrants to neighborhoods by nationality
Housing laws require it
Each neighborhood was built by one country's government
Migrants follow relatives and neighbors who came earlier
check.why: That is chain migration: the first arrivals write home, and later migrants go where they already know someone.

lessons.title: The Great Migration to Chicago
lessons.mainIdea: Between 1910 and 1970 about six million Black Americans left the South, and Chicago became one of their main destinations.
reading: In 1910 about forty-four thousand Black people lived in Chicago. By 1920 there were roughly one hundred nine thousand, and by 1930 about two hundred thirty-four thousand. This was the start of the *Great Migration*, the movement of about six million African Americans out of the South between 1910 and 1970. It was one of the largest internal migrations in American history, and it was driven by a clear set of pushes and pulls.

The pushes were brutal. Under Jim Crow laws, Black Southerners could not vote, were forced into segregated and inferior schools, and lived under the threat of lynching. Most farmed as sharecroppers, renting land and paying with a share of the crop, a system that kept families in permanent debt. In the 1910s the boll weevil, a beetle, destroyed cotton crops across the South, wiping out even that thin living.

The pulls came from the North. World War I cut off immigration from Europe just as factories needed workers, so Chicago's steel mills, stockyards and railroads hired Black workers for the first time in large numbers. A job in a Chicago packinghouse paid several times what a sharecropper earned. The Chicago Defender, a Black newspaper carried south by railroad porters, printed job ads and stories of Northern life and urged readers to come. Letters home did the rest.

The obstacles did not disappear when the trains pulled into the Illinois Central station. Chicago confined Black families to a narrow strip on the South Side that became known as the Black Belt, through restrictive covenants that barred selling homes to Black buyers and through violence when they moved beyond it. In the summer of 1919 a riot killed thirty-eight people. Yet the migrants built churches, businesses, newspapers and music, and Chicago blues and gospel are among the results. A migration reshapes both the place people leave and the place they arrive.

words.d: the movement of about six million Black Americans from the South to Northern and Western cities between 1910 and 1970
a farmer who rents land and pays with part of the crop, a system that often trapped families in debt
a clause in a property deed that barred selling or renting to people of certain races

look.title: Chicago's Black Population
look.prompt: Between which two censuses did the Black population grow fastest in percentage terms? What was happening in the world in those years?

check.q: Which was a PUSH factor in the Great Migration?
choices: Jim Crow laws and the threat of lynching
Ads in the Chicago Defender
Factory jobs in Chicago's stockyards
Relatives already living on the South Side
check.why: Jim Crow and violence drove people out of the South. The other three drew people toward Chicago.

check.q: Why did Northern factories start hiring Black workers in large numbers during the 1910s?
choices: A new federal law required it
World War I cut off immigrant workers from Europe
Southern states paid factories to take workers
Factories moved south to find them
check.why: The war stopped European immigration just as demand for workers rose, so employers turned to Black Southerners.

check.q: What was the Black Belt in Chicago?
choices: A railroad line from Mississippi
A farming region south of the city
A narrow South Side strip where Black families were confined
A labor union for packinghouse workers
check.why: Covenants and violence kept Black Chicagoans within a narrow strip of the South Side, which came to be called the Black Belt.

lessons.title: Migration Today
lessons.mainIdea: International migration today is driven by wages, war and family, and Illinois's population depends on it.
reading: About 280 million people now live outside the country where they were born. That is roughly three and a half percent of humanity. The United States has more immigrants than any other country, about forty-five million. Several smaller countries, though, have a higher share. The largest single flow in the world runs from Mexico to the United States. Other big flows run from South Asia to the oil states of the Persian Gulf, from North Africa and the Middle East into Europe, and from Ukraine after Russia's invasion in 2022.

Most of this is economic. Ravenstein's short-distance rule still holds inside countries, but the pull of a wage five or ten times higher can overcome an ocean. Migrants send money home, called remittances, and for countries like the Philippines, Guatemala and Nepal those transfers are one of the biggest sources of income. Most migrants are young adults, which is why they tend to fill jobs in construction, farming, care work and restaurants in the places they arrive.

War drives the rest. The United Nations counted more than 100 million forcibly displaced people in 2022, the most ever recorded. Some are refugees who crossed a border, from Syria, Afghanistan, Ukraine, Venezuela, South Sudan and Myanmar among others. More are internally displaced, uprooted but still inside their own country. Most refugees do not go to rich countries; they stay next door, in Turkey, Colombia, Pakistan, Uganda and Germany. Whether a migrant counts as a refugee or an economic migrant decides what rights they have, and the line is often argued.

Illinois is a case study. The state has about 1.8 million foreign-born residents, roughly one in seven people. Mexico, India, Poland, the Philippines and China are the leading birthplaces. Without them the state's population would be falling, since Illinois has more people leaving for other states than arriving from them. Debates about migration in Illinois, like everywhere, turn on real trade-offs: wages and jobs, the cost of schools and services, and the law. Behind all of it is a simple fact: every migrant is a person who left home for a reason.

words.d: money a migrant sends home to family in the country they came from
someone forced from home by war or disaster who has not crossed a national border
a resident who was born in another country, whether or not they have become a citizen

look.title: Words on a Pedestal
look.text: Give me your tired, your poor, / Your huddled masses yearning to breathe free, / The wretched refuse of your teeming shore. / Send these, the homeless, tempest-tost to me, / I lift my lamp beside the golden door!
look.cite: Emma Lazarus, The New Colossus, 1883, placed on the Statue of Liberty in 1903
look.prompt: Lazarus wrote these lines about the same time Congress passed the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882. What does that pairing tell you about American attitudes toward migrants?

check.q: What is a remittance?
choices: A fee a migrant pays to cross a border
A tax on foreign-born workers
A government payment to refugees
Money a migrant sends home to family
check.why: Remittances flow from migrants back to their home countries and are a major source of income for some nations.

check.q: Where do MOST refugees end up living?
choices: In countries next door to the one they fled
In the United States
In refugee camps run by the United Nations in Europe
Back in their own homes within a year
check.why: The reading notes that most refugees stay in neighboring countries such as Turkey, Colombia and Pakistan.

check.q: Why does Illinois's population depend on immigration?
choices: Illinois has the highest birth rate in the country
More people leave Illinois for other states than arrive from them
Illinois bans people from moving to other states
Illinois has no foreign-born residents
check.why: Illinois loses residents to other states, so arrivals from abroad are what keep its population from shrinking.

lessons.title: Language Families on the Map
lessons.mainIdea: The world's roughly seven thousand languages descend from a smaller number of families, and their map records ancient migrations and modern empires.
reading: Linguists count about seven thousand living languages. Most are spoken by small groups, and hundreds have fewer than a thousand speakers left. A handful are giants: Mandarin Chinese has close to a billion native speakers, Spanish about half a billion, and English roughly four hundred million native speakers plus far more who learned it later. Languages that share a common ancestor form a *language family*, the way cousins share a grandparent.

The largest family by speakers is *Indo-European*, which stretches from Iceland to Bangladesh and includes English, Spanish, Russian, Persian, Hindi and Bengali. English mother, German Mutter, Latin mater, Sanskrit matar: the resemblance is not chance. These languages all descend from one spoken on the grasslands north of the Black Sea perhaps six thousand years ago. Sino-Tibetan, including Chinese, is the second largest family. Others include Afro-Asiatic, with Arabic and Hebrew; Niger-Congo, with Swahili and Yoruba; and Austronesian, whose speakers sailed from Taiwan to Madagascar, Hawaii and New Zealand.

A language spreads by *diffusion*. Relocation diffusion happens when speakers move, which is how English reached North America and Spanish reached the Andes. Expansion diffusion happens when a language spreads to new people without a mass migration, the way Latin spread through the Roman Empire or English spreads today through trade, science and the internet. Conquest, colonization and schooling have carried a few languages across the world while pushing many others toward extinction.

Illinois shows both patterns. The state's name comes from a French version of a word used by the Illinois people, an Algonquian-speaking nation. French traders and priests named Des Plaines, Vincennes and Bourbonnais. English arrived with American settlers. Today about a quarter of Chicago households speak a language other than English at home, Spanish most of all, followed by Polish, Chinese, Tagalog and Arabic. A city's street signs are a record of who came, and when.

words.d: a group of languages that descend from a common ancestor language
the largest language family by speakers, including English, Spanish, Russian, Persian and Hindi
the spread of an idea, practice or language from one place to others

look.title: Native Speakers of the Big Languages
look.cite: Ethnologue and standard estimates, about 2022, rounded
look.prompt: English ranks third by native speakers but first as a second language. Why might a language become the world's most learned second language without being the most spoken first language?

check.q: What makes two languages part of the same family?
choices: They are spoken in the same country
They use the same alphabet
They descend from a common ancestor language
They have the same number of speakers
check.why: A family is defined by shared descent, like cousins with the same grandparent. English and Hindi are in the same family though they look very different.

check.q: English reached North America mainly through which kind of diffusion?
choices: Expansion diffusion by trade
Hierarchical diffusion from cities to farms
Contagious diffusion by the internet
Relocation diffusion by migration
check.why: English speakers physically moved across the Atlantic and settled, which is relocation diffusion.

check.q: Which fact best shows that Illinois has many layers of language history?
choices: Its place names come from Algonquian, French and English
Illinois has the most English speakers of any state
All Illinois schools teach Spanish
Chicago was founded by Polish immigrants
check.why: The reading traces the state's name to the Illinois people, French names like Des Plaines, and later English settlement.

lessons.title: Religion on the Map
lessons.mainIdea: The world's major religions each have a geography: a hearth where they began, routes by which they spread, and a landscape they shape.
reading: Roughly a third of the world's people identify as Christian, about two and a third billion. Nearly two billion are Muslim, about 1.2 billion are Hindu, and about half a billion are Buddhist. Around 1.2 billion say they belong to no religion, a group concentrated in China, Japan and parts of Europe. Judaism has about fifteen million followers but an outsized place in history, since Christianity and Islam both grew from its soil. Hundreds of millions more follow folk, traditional and smaller faiths.

Each faith has a *hearth*, the place it began. Judaism, Christianity and Islam all began in Southwest Asia, within a few hundred miles of one another. Hinduism and Buddhism began in the Indian subcontinent. From the hearth, religions spread the same ways languages do. Missionaries and traders carried Buddhism along the Silk Roads to China, Korea and Japan, and Islam along sea routes to Indonesia, now the largest Muslim-majority country. Conquest and colonization carried Christianity to the Americas and much of Africa. Hinduism spread far less, because it is tied to particular places, rivers and communities in India.

Geographers distinguish *universalizing religions*, which seek converts from anyone anywhere, from ethnic religions, which are bound to one people and place. Christianity, Islam and Buddhism are universalizing, which is why they cover the map. Hinduism, Judaism and Shinto are mostly ethnic religions. The distinction helps explain the pattern: a faith that sends missionaries spreads like ink; a faith you are born into moves only when its people move.

Religion writes itself on the landscape. A Chicago skyline holds church steeples and the domes of Orthodox cathedrals built by Greek and Ukrainian immigrants. There are minarets of mosques on the Southwest Side and in suburbs like Bridgeview. Hindu temples stand in Lemont and Aurora. The Baha'i House of Worship in Wilmette is one of only a few in the world. Cemeteries, holidays, food rules, and the days shops close all follow the same map. Religion is one of the strongest forces shaping where people gather and how they live together.

words.d: the place where a culture trait such as a religion or language first began
a religion that seeks to convert people anywhere, such as Christianity, Islam or Buddhism
a religion tied to one people and place, such as Hinduism, Judaism or Shinto

look.title: Followers of the World's Largest Faiths
look.cite: Pew Research Center estimates, about 2020, rounded
look.prompt: Islam is growing faster than any other large religion, mainly because Muslim populations are younger. How does that connect to the population pyramids at the start of this chapter?

check.q: Why is Hinduism found mostly in one region while Christianity is found worldwide?
choices: Hinduism is much newer
Hinduism is an ethnic religion tied to place; Christianity is universalizing
Christianity has fewer followers
Hindus were not allowed to travel
check.why: Universalizing faiths seek converts everywhere and so spread widely; ethnic faiths move only when their people move.

check.q: How did Islam reach Indonesia?
choices: Through European colonization
Through Roman conquest
Through sea trade routes
Through the Silk Roads by land
check.why: The reading says traders carried Islam along sea routes to Indonesia, which is now the largest Muslim-majority country.

check.q: What is a religion's hearth?
choices: Its largest temple
The country with the most followers today
The route by which it spread
The place where it began
check.why: A hearth is an origin point. Southwest Asia is the hearth of Judaism, Christianity and Islam.

lessons.title: Ethnicity, Identity and Conflict
lessons.mainIdea: Ethnic identity is built from shared history, language and culture, and when borders and power ignore it the result can be division or violence.
reading: An *ethnic group* is a set of people who see themselves as sharing a common ancestry, history, language, or culture. Ethnicity is not the same as race, which sorts people by physical appearance. It is not the same as nationality either, which is citizenship in a state. A person can be ethnically Kurdish, a citizen of Turkey, and speak Turkish at school. Ethnicity is partly inherited and partly chosen, and it can shift over generations. That is why the grandchildren of Chicago's Italian, Irish and Polish immigrants today mostly describe themselves simply as American.

Trouble comes when the lines on a map do not match the people inside them. Most of the borders in Africa and the Middle East were drawn by European powers between the 1880s and 1920s with little regard for who lived where. The Kurds, roughly thirty million people, were split among Turkey, Iraq, Iran and Syria. They have no state of their own. When Britain left India in 1947 it divided the land into India and Pakistan along religious lines. Roughly fifteen million people fled across the new border in a few months, and hundreds of thousands died in the violence.

The worst outcomes have names. Ethnic cleansing is the forced removal of a group from a territory. Genocide is the deliberate attempt to destroy a group. In Rwanda in 1994, over about one hundred days, Hutu extremists killed roughly eight hundred thousand people, mostly Tutsi, in a country where the two groups spoke the same language and lived side by side. In the former Yugoslavia in the 1990s, wars over which people belonged where killed more than one hundred thousand.

Yet ethnic diversity is not the cause of conflict by itself. Switzerland has four national languages and has been at peace for generations. Chicago has Mexican, Black, Polish, Chinese, Indian, Arab and Ukrainian neighborhoods within a few miles of one another. The difference lies in whether a state treats all groups fairly, whether power is shared, and whether leaders choose to inflame differences or manage them. Geography sets the stage; politics writes the script.

words.d: people who identify with one another through shared ancestry, history, language or culture
the forced removal of an ethnic group from a territory
the deliberate attempt to destroy a national, ethnic, racial or religious group

look.title: A Line Through a Village
look.text: Imagine a surveyor in 1885 drawing a straight border across a map of Africa in a meeting room in Berlin. On the ground, the line passes through the middle of a village whose people share one language, one market and one set of grandparents. Sixty years later that line becomes the boundary between two independent countries with different official languages, currencies and armies.
look.prompt: List three concrete problems the people of that village would face. Then suggest one way the two new governments could reduce the harm.

check.q: How is ethnicity different from nationality?
choices: Ethnicity is shared ancestry and culture; nationality is citizenship in a state
Ethnicity is citizenship; nationality is culture
They mean exactly the same thing
Ethnicity is chosen; nationality is inherited
check.why: A Kurd can be a Turkish citizen. Nationality is a legal status; ethnicity is shared identity and culture.

check.q: What happened when British India was divided in 1947?
choices: The border followed old ethnic lines and there was little disruption
About fifteen million people crossed the new border amid deadly violence
India and Pakistan agreed to share one government
The Kurds received their own state
check.why: Partition along religious lines forced millions to flee and hundreds of thousands died, an example of borders ignoring the people within them.

check.q: According to the reading, what best explains why some diverse countries are peaceful and others are not?
choices: How many ethnic groups they contain
Whether they are in Africa or Europe
Whether power is shared and groups are treated fairly
Whether they have a single official language
check.why: Switzerland and Chicago show that diversity alone does not cause conflict; fair treatment and political choices make the difference.

lessons.title: Folk Culture, Pop Culture and Landscape
lessons.mainIdea: Folk culture is local and slow to change, popular culture spreads fast and wide, and both leave their marks on the landscape.
reading: Culture is everything a group of people learns and passes on: food, clothing, houses, music, games, beliefs and manners. Geographers split it roughly in two. *Folk culture* belongs to a small, usually rural group, changes slowly, and is passed down in person. The Amish of central Illinois, with their horse-drawn buggies and plain dress, keep a folk culture on purpose. So do the quilting patterns, fiddle tunes and barn styles that vary from one valley to the next in Appalachia.

*Popular culture* is the opposite. It is produced for a mass market, spreads fast through media and trade, and looks much the same everywhere. A fast-food chain in Chicago, Cairo and Tokyo serves nearly the same menu. The same songs top charts on several continents in the same week. Pop culture diffuses hierarchically, jumping from big cities to smaller ones and skipping the countryside at first, and then contagiously, spreading person to person like a cold. Both kinds of culture are real culture; the difference is scale and speed.

Every culture writes itself on the land. Geographers call the result the *cultural landscape*: the visible marks people leave, from field patterns to skylines. Chicago's bungalow belt, tens of thousands of brick single-family homes built between about 1910 and 1940, is a cultural landscape. So is the corn-and-soybean checkerboard of central Illinois, laid out on the square-mile grid that the Land Ordinance of 1785 imposed on the whole Midwest. So are the murals of Pilsen and the shrines in front yards on the Southwest Side.

The spread of popular culture raises real questions. When a global brand replaces local food, or English crowds out a language with five hundred speakers, something is lost that cannot be rebuilt. At the same time, popular culture carries new ideas, connects people across borders, and gives young people in small towns a window on the world. Geographers do not settle that argument; they map it, and ask who gains and who loses in each place.

words.d: the traditions of a small, usually rural group, passed on in person and slow to change
mass-produced culture that spreads quickly through media and trade and looks similar everywhere
the visible marks that a culture leaves on the land, from field patterns to buildings

look.title: Two Kitchens
look.text: In one kitchen a grandmother in southern Illinois makes a dumpling recipe her German great-grandmother brought in the 1850s; she has never written it down. In another kitchen a teenager three miles away follows a recipe from a video posted yesterday by a cook in Seoul, and by next week a million people have made the same dish.
look.prompt: Which kitchen is folk culture and which is popular culture? What would it take for each recipe to still be made in fifty years?

check.q: Which is the best example of folk culture?
choices: A fast-food chain with the same menu worldwide
A song that tops charts on three continents
A video game played by millions
Quilting patterns passed down within one Appalachian valley
check.why: Folk culture is local, passed on in person and slow to change, which fits the quilting tradition.

check.q: Popular culture usually spreads FIRST to
choices: Big cities, then smaller places
Rural villages, then cities
Every place at the same moment
Only places with the same language
check.why: The reading describes hierarchical diffusion: pop culture jumps between big cities before reaching the countryside.

check.q: Why do central Illinois farm fields form a checkerboard of squares?
choices: Corn grows best in square fields
The Land Ordinance of 1785 laid a square-mile grid on the Midwest
Glaciers carved the land into squares
Railroads required square fields
check.why: The 1785 survey grid divided the land into square-mile sections, and roads and fields still follow it.

lessons.title: Gender and Development
lessons.mainIdea: Where girls are educated and women can work and own property, birth rates fall, incomes rise and whole societies develop faster.
reading: Look back at the two pyramids. The single strongest predictor of a country's birth rate is how many years its girls spend in school. Across the world, women who finish secondary school marry later, have fewer children, and are far more likely to see those children survive. In Niger, where most women have little schooling, the average woman has about six children. In neighboring countries where girls' education has expanded, the rate has dropped much faster. Education changes what women can choose.

Geographers measure these gaps directly. Literacy rates for women still trail those for men in much of South Asia and sub-Saharan Africa, though the gap has narrowed sharply since 1990. Women do most of the world's unpaid work, farming, hauling water, and caring for children and the old, which does not show up in a country's income statistics at all. In many countries women cannot legally own land or open a bank account without a male relative's permission. The United Nations tracks these differences in a Gender Inequality Index that combines health, schooling, jobs and political power.

Development moves when the gaps close. Economists have found that when women earn income, a larger share of it goes to children's food and schooling. Women in Bangladesh's garment factories, whatever the hard conditions, have driven a sharp fall in early marriage and birth rates since the 1990s. Rwanda, rebuilding after the 1994 genocide, wrote quotas for women into its constitution and now has one of the highest shares of women in any national legislature, above sixty percent.

The United States is not finished with these questions either. American women earn on average about eighty-two cents for every dollar men earn, partly because of the jobs they hold and partly because of pay for the same job. Women hold about a quarter of the seats in Congress. Illinois has elected women to the U.S. Senate and to the state's top offices, and women make up more than half of the state's college students. Development, here as anywhere, is not just about roads and factories; it is about who gets to use them.

words.d: the share of adults who can read and write a simple sentence
a United Nations measure combining differences between women and men in health, education, work and political power
labor such as farming for the family, hauling water and caring for children that earns no wage and is not counted in income statistics

look.title: Girls' Schooling and Family Size
look.prompt: Bangladesh had a fertility rate near seven in 1970 and is now below two. What changes in women's lives would you look for to explain such a fast drop?

check.q: According to the reading, what is the strongest predictor of a country's birth rate?
choices: Its total land area
The size of its army
How many years its girls spend in school
Its main religion
check.why: Women who finish secondary school marry later and have fewer children, and this holds across regions and faiths.

check.q: Why does much of women's work not appear in income statistics?
choices: Because women do not work in most countries
Because governments refuse to count women
Because statistics only count city jobs
Because it is unpaid, such as farming for the family and hauling water
check.why: Unpaid labor at home and on family farms earns no wage, so income measures miss it even though it keeps households alive.

check.q: What did Rwanda do after 1994 that changed women's political power?
choices: It wrote quotas for women into its constitution
It moved its capital
It banned women from voting
It joined the European Union
check.why: Constitutional quotas helped make Rwanda's legislature one of the most female in the world, above sixty percent.

review.q: Which region of the world has one of the HIGHEST population densities?
choices: Central Australia
The Ganges valley of India
Siberia
The Sahara
review.why: The Ganges valley is warm, wet and fertile and holds hundreds of millions of people; the other three are dry, cold or both.

review.q: In stage two of the demographic transition, a population grows rapidly because
choices: Birth rates rise sharply
Immigration increases
Death rates fall while birth rates stay high
Families move to cities
review.why: Falling deaths with unchanged births create the gap that produces rapid growth.

review.q: A population pyramid with a narrow base and a thick top most likely belongs to
choices: Nigeria
Niger
India
Japan
review.why: Japan has few children and many elderly, giving its pyramid a narrow bottom and a thick top.

review.q: Which of these was a PULL factor in the Great Migration?
choices: Jobs in Chicago packinghouses
Sharecropping debt
Lynching
The boll weevil destroying cotton
review.why: Jobs drew people toward Chicago; the other three pushed people out of the South.

review.q: The Kurds are an example of
choices: A universalizing religion
An ethnic group split among several states with no state of their own
A language family
A refugee agency
review.why: About thirty million Kurds live divided among Turkey, Iraq, Iran and Syria, a case of borders that ignore ethnicity.

review.q: English, Hindi and Spanish all belong to which language family?
choices: Afro-Asiatic
Sino-Tibetan
Indo-European
Austronesian
review.why: All three descend from a common ancestor spoken north of the Black Sea, making them Indo-European.

review.q: Which statement about religion and geography is TRUE?
choices: Hinduism spread worldwide through missionaries
Islam reached Indonesia through European colonization
Buddhism began in China
Judaism, Christianity and Islam all have hearths in Southwest Asia
review.why: The three faiths began within a few hundred miles of one another in Southwest Asia. Buddhism began in India and Islam reached Indonesia by sea trade.

review.q: Which change would most likely LOWER a country's birth rate, based on this chapter?
choices: Keeping girls in school through secondary level
Building more farms
Raising the number of men in the army
Lowering the death rate among the elderly
review.why: Girls' schooling is the strongest predictor of lower fertility, as the Bangladesh and Niger examples show.
